Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 49, verses 4–8:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers, most of them do not understand.﴾ ﴿And if they had been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, if a deviator brings you news, verify it, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful.﴾ ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah. If he were to obey you in much of the matter, you would be in difficulty. But Allah has endeared to you the faith and made it beautiful in your hearts, and He has made hateful to you disbelief, defiance, and disobedience. Those are the rightly guided.﴾ ﴿A bounty from Allah and a favor. And Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you﴾ up to His saying: "Forgiving and Merciful." It was revealed concerning the delegation of Banu Tamim, among whom were al-Aqra' ibn Habis, al-Zibriqan ibn Badr, 'Amr ibn al-Ahtam, and others. The occasion was that "they came as a delegation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), entered the mosque, and approached the chambers of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), which were nine. They began calling out without waiting, and all of them called out together: 'O Muhammad, come out to us! O Muhammad, come out to us!' Their conduct contained rudeness, crudeness, and little respect. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) waited for a period, then came out to them. Al-Aqra' ibn Habis said to him: 'O Muhammad, indeed my praise is an adornment and my blame is a disgrace.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'Woe to you, that is Allah, the Exalted.' The people gathered in the mosque, and their orator stood and gave a speech and boasted. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, may Allah be pleased with him, and he gave a speech, mentioned Allah the Exalted and Islam, and surpassed their orator. Then their poet stood and recited, boasting, and Hassan ibn Thabit, may Allah be pleased with him, stood and boasted by Allah the Exalted, by the Messenger (ﷺ), and by valor, and he was more eloquent than their poet. Some of them said to others: 'By Allah, this man is indeed supported (mu'tan lahu), his orator is more eloquent than our orator, and his poet is more eloquent than our poet.' Then this verse was revealed concerning them."

This is a summary of what the narrations agree upon concerning this verse. Musa ibn 'Uqba narrated it from Abu Salama, from al-Aqra' ibn Habis. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, the reading is: "most of them are Banu Tamim who do not understand."

"Al-hujurat" is the plural of "hujra." The majority of reciters read "al-hujurat" with a damma on the ha' and the jim. Abu Ja'far the reciter alone read "al-hujarat" with a fatha on the jim. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿it would have been better for them﴾ means in reward with Allah the Exalted, and in the Prophet's (ﷺ) ease of spirit, his fulfilling their needs, and his affection for them. All of that is good, though without doubt some of it was withheld because of their rudeness. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is an encouragement for them and an announcement that He accepts the repentance of the penitent and forgives and shows mercy to whoever turns back and returns.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, if a deviator brings you news﴾ and the rest of the verse. Its occasion was that "the Prophet (ﷺ) sent al-Walid ibn 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt to Banu al-Mustaliq as a collector of alms (musaddiqan)." It is reported that he was hostile toward them and wished to harm them, so he turned back from part of his route and lied about them (this was said by al-Dahhak), and he told the Prophet (ﷺ): "They refused me the alms, drove me away, and apostatized." The Prophet (ﷺ) became angry and intended to fight them, and he deliberated on the matter and sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to them. Their delegation met him, denying that. It is narrated from Umm Salama and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, that when al-Walid ibn 'Uqba drew near to them, they came out to meet him. He saw them from a distance, became frightened of them, suspected evil from them, and turned back, and he said what we have mentioned. It is also narrated that when he drew near to them, he was informed that they had said: "We will neither give him the alms nor give him anything." He acted upon the soundness of this report and turned back and said what we have mentioned. The verse was revealed for this cause. Al-Walid, according to what Mujahid and Qatada mentioned, is the one referred to as "the deviator." Al-Zahrawi related that Umm Salama said: "He is al-Walid ibn 'Uqba." Then the verse remains applicable to whoever possesses this attribute throughout time. "Al-fisq" (deviance) is departure from the path of truth, and it has differing degrees, all of which are grounds for lying and call for verification and clarification. Qatada, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, used to say: "Allah the Exalted has said to the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah. If he were to obey you in much of the matter, you would be in difficulty﴾. By Allah, you were less sound in judgment and more hasty in understanding. So let a man distrust himself and seek counsel from the Book of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 49, verses 4–8:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers, most of them do not understand.﴾ ﴿And if they had been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, if a deviator brings you news, verify it, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful.﴾ ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah. If he were to obey you in much of the matter, you would be in difficulty. But Allah has endeared to you the faith and made it beautiful in your hearts, and He has made hateful to you disbelief, defiance, and disobedience. Those are the rightly guided.﴾ ﴿A bounty from Allah and a favor. And Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you﴾ up to His saying: "Forgiving and Merciful." It was revealed concerning the delegation of Banu Tamim, among whom were al-Aqra' ibn Habis, al-Zibriqan ibn Badr, 'Amr ibn al-Ahtam, and others. The occasion was that "they came as a delegation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), entered the mosque, and approached the chambers of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), which were nine. They began calling out without waiting, and all of them called out together: 'O Muhammad, come out to us! O Muhammad, come out to us!' Their conduct contained rudeness, crudeness, and little respect. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) waited for a period, then came out to them. Al-Aqra' ibn Habis said to him: 'O Muhammad, indeed my praise is an adornment and my blame is a disgrace.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'Woe to you, that is Allah, the Exalted.' The people gathered in the mosque, and their orator stood and gave a speech and boasted. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, may Allah be pleased with him, and he gave a speech, mentioned Allah the Exalted and Islam, and surpassed their orator. Then their poet stood and recited, boasting, and Hassan ibn Thabit, may Allah be pleased with him, stood and boasted by Allah the Exalted, by the Messenger (ﷺ), and by valor, and he was more eloquent than their poet. Some of them said to others: 'By Allah, this man is indeed supported (mu'tan lahu), his orator is more eloquent than our orator, and his poet is more eloquent than our poet.' Then this verse was revealed concerning them."

This is a summary of what the narrations agree upon concerning this verse. Musa ibn 'Uqba narrated it from Abu Salama, from al-Aqra' ibn Habis. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, the reading is: "most of them are Banu Tamim who do not understand."

"Al-hujurat" is the plural of "hujra." The majority of reciters read "al-hujurat" with a damma on the ha' and the jim. Abu Ja'far the reciter alone read "al-hujarat" with a fatha on the jim. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿it would have been better for them﴾ means in reward with Allah the Exalted, and in the Prophet's (ﷺ) ease of spirit, his fulfilling their needs, and his affection for them. All of that is good, though without doubt some of it was withheld because of their rudeness. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is an encouragement for them and an announcement that He accepts the repentance of the penitent and forgives and shows mercy to whoever turns back and returns.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, if a deviator brings you news﴾ and the rest of the verse. Its occasion was that "the Prophet (ﷺ) sent al-Walid ibn 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt to Banu al-Mustaliq as a collector of alms (musaddiqan)." It is reported that he was hostile toward them and wished to harm them, so he turned back from part of his route and lied about them (this was said by al-Dahhak), and he told the Prophet (ﷺ): "They refused me the alms, drove me away, and apostatized." The Prophet (ﷺ) became angry and intended to fight them, and he deliberated on the matter and sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to them. Their delegation met him, denying that. It is narrated from Umm Salama and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, that when al-Walid ibn 'Uqba drew near to them, they came out to meet him. He saw them from a distance, became frightened of them, suspected evil from them, and turned back, and he said what we have mentioned. It is also narrated that when he drew near to them, he was informed that they had said: "We will neither give him the alms nor give him anything." He acted upon the soundness of this report and turned back and said what we have mentioned. The verse was revealed for this cause. Al-Walid, according to what Mujahid and Qatada mentioned, is the one referred to as "the deviator." Al-Zahrawi related that Umm Salama said: "He is al-Walid ibn 'Uqba." Then the verse remains applicable to whoever possesses this attribute throughout time. "Al-fisq" (deviance) is departure from the path of truth, and it has differing degrees, all of which are grounds for lying and call for verification and clarification. Those who hold that the report of a single narrator is accepted found support in what the implication of this verse (dalil al-khitab) requires, because it implies that someone who is not a deviator, when he brings news, should act upon it. This is not a strong argument, and this is not the place to discuss the question of the single narrator's report.

The majority of reciters read "fa-tabayyanu" from "tabayyun" (clarification). Hamza, al-Hasan, Ibn Wththab, Talha, al-A'mash, and 'Isa read "fa-tathabbatu" (verify). The "an" in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿lest you harm﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), as if He, the Exalted, said: "for fear that you harm." Qatada said: "When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Verification is from Allah, and haste is from Satan.'" Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: This verse refutes those who say that all Muslims are upright (ʿudul) until discrediting (jarh) is established, because Allah the Exalted commanded clarification before acceptance.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

His saying implies that someone whose state is unknown is feared to be a deviator, and caution is required. Al-Naqqash said: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿fa-tabayyanu﴾ is more emphatic than "tathabbatu," because one may verify without clarifying.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah﴾ is a rebuke to the liars and a warning of exposure. That is, let the liar consider that Allah will expose him through the tongue of His Messenger (ﷺ). Then He said: ﴿If he were to obey you in much of the matter, you would be in difficulty﴾, that is, you would be wretched and ruined. "Al-'anat" means hardship. That is, if he were to obey you, O believers, in much of what you see through your own reasoning and your going ahead of him. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But Allah has endeared to you the faith﴾ and the rest of the verse, is as if He, the Exalted, said: "But Allah has bestowed such-and-such favors," and in that is sufficiency and a matter you cannot fully repay with gratitude. So do not go ahead in matters, and be content with Allah's blessing upon you. Allah the Blessed and Exalted endeared the faith and made it beautiful by placing love for it and goodness in the hearts of the believers. Likewise, He made disbelief, defiance, and disobedience hateful. Al-Rummani related from al-Hasan that He endeared the faith by what He described of its reward, and made hateful the three opposites of faith by what He described of the punishment for them. If he were to obey you in much of the matter, you would be in difficulty﴾. By Allah, you were less sound in judgment and more hasty in understanding. So let a man distrust himself and seek counsel from the Book of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted."

"Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 49, verse 9–10:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, then make peace between them. But if one of them oppresses the other, then fight the one that oppresses until it returns to the command of Allah. And if it returns, then make peace between them with justice and act equitably. Indeed, Allah loves those who act equitably.﴾ ﴿The believers are but brothers, so make settlement between your two brothers and fear Allah that you may receive mercy.﴾

"Ṭāʾifatān" is in the nominative case, governed by an implied verb. The ṭāʾifah (a group, sect) means a company, and it may also be applied to a single individual. In support of this, he cited His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Why did not a group from every division of them go forth?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122]. Some people held that the testimony of a single man suffices for the two hadd witnesses of adulterers; this verse, according to them, has a single ruling whether applied to individuals or to groups.

The people differed concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse. Anas ibn Mālik and the majority said: its occasion was what took place between the Muslims and those of them who were partisan with ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl, when «the Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed by him while he was heading to visit Saʿd ibn ʿUbādah, may Allah be pleased with him, during his illness. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy said, when the donkey of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came close to him: "Do not raise dust upon us; the stench of your donkey has harmed us." ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥah, may Allah be pleased with him, replied to him, and the hadith is given in full. The people quarrelled until blows were exchanged with palm stalks, and it is also narrated "with iron."»

Abū Mālik and al-Ḥasan said: its occasion was that two groups of the Anṣār fought with one another, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ settled the matter after great effort, and the verse was revealed concerning that.

As-Suddī said: there was in Medina a woman from the Anṣār called Umm Badr, who had a husband from another people. Something occurred between them which caused her people to be incensed on her behalf and his people on his behalf, and fighting broke out; the verse was revealed on account of it.

"Baghat" means: it sought exaltation without right. Repelling the oppressing group is obligatory in every circumstance, but preparing to fight it is under the authority of the rulers. It was said to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him: "Are the people of Ṣiffīn and the Camel polytheists?" He said: "No, they fled from polytheism." It was asked: "Are they hypocrites?" He said: "No, for the hypocrites do not remember Allah except a little." It was asked: "Then what is their state?" He said: "They are our brothers who have oppressed us." The Prophet ﷺ said: «The ruling of Allah, Exalted is He, concerning the oppressing group is that one should not finish off the wounded, nor pursue the fleeing, nor kill the captive.»

"Tafīʾa" means: returns; and "al-iqsāṭ" (acting equitably) means: judging with justice.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ means brothers in religion. The majority of the readers recited "bayna akhawaykum" (between your two brothers), in consideration of the least number in which fighting and quarrelling occur; and when a group intends reconciliation, it is in fact between two men, two men. Ibn ʿĀmir and al-Ḥasan (in one of the reports from him) recited "bayna ikhwatikum" (between your brothers). Ibn Masʿūd, Zayd ibn Thābit, Ibn Sīrīn, al-Ḥasan, ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī, Thābit al-Bunānī and Ḥammād ibn Salamah recited "bayna ikhwānikum" (between your brothers), and it is a good reading, because the plural of akh (brother) in religion or similar, not by lineage, is most commonly ikhwān, while for lineage it is most commonly ikhwah and ikhāʾ. The poet said:

You found your brother among us when you forgot, and which of the sons of brotherhood has a kinship that is disowned?

These plurals may overlap, and all of them occur in the Book of Allah, Exalted is He. Of it is: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾, and of it is "or the houses of your brothers" (al-Nūr: 61). This latter usage is the less common.»"

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 49, verses 11–12:

The words of the Exalted:

﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people; perhaps they may be better than them, nor let women ridicule [other] women; perhaps they may be better than them. And do not defame one another, nor insult each other by nicknames. Wretched is the name of defiance after belief. And whoever does not repent, then it is those who are the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, avoid much of [negative] assumption, for indeed some assumption is sin. And do not spy, and do not backbite one another. Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would detest it. And fear Allah; indeed Allah is Accepting of repentance and Merciful.﴾

These verses and those that follow were revealed concerning the character of the people of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance). That is because they followed the desires of their souls, and no command or prohibition from Allah the Exalted restrained them. So a man would ridicule, defame, and insult others with nicknames, and he would entertain suspicions, speak of them, backbite, boast, and so on, among the other base traits of the corrupt souls. Then this verse was revealed as a discipline for the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Some people have mentioned causes (asbab al-nuzul) for these verses. Among what has been said: the verse "let not a people ridicule" was revealed because of 'Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl. He used to walk in Madinah armed, and a people said to him, "This is the Pharaoh of this community," and that displeased him, so he complained of it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). But my firm opinion is that this verse was revealed as a correction for all creation, and if you were to trace the causes, they would be more than can be counted.

"Yaskhar" means to mock (yastahzi'). Mockery arises when a person is weak, whether because of youth, a recent illness, a calamity, or a flaw he commits. So the believers are forbidden from mocking in these matters and others, a general prohibition. Indeed, the one mocked may be better than the mocker. In the speech of the Arabs, "qawm" (people) applies to males, and it is among the collective nouns like "rahT" (a band of men). Some have said it derives from "qiyam" (standing), or is the plural of "qa'im" (standing) as "da'if" (weak). From this is the verse of the poet, Zuhayr:

"And I do not know, and I suppose I will never know, whether the family of Hisn are a 'qawm' or 'nisa'."

This verse implies that "qawm" is specific to males, though a group of males may include women, in which case they are called "qawm" by giving precedence to the status of the males. Then Allah the Exalted forbade women from what He forbade men of that. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud recited: "'asaw an yakunu" and "'asayna an yakunna."

"Talmizu" means that some of you disparage others by mentioning their faults and the like. Al-lamz may be by speech, by gesture, and the like, of what another person understands. Al-hamz, however, is only by the tongue. It is likened to striking (hamz) with a stick or the like, which requires contact. The poet said:

"And whose glory we have struck, he has become humbled."

It was said to a Bedouin, "Do you strike (tahmizu) the mouse?" He said, "The cat strikes it." Al-Tha'labi related that al-lamz is what is done in a person's presence, and al-hamz is what is done in his absence. Al-Zahrawi related from 'Ali ibn Sulayman the opposite of that, saying: al-hamz is to find fault in his presence, and al-lamz is in his absence. From this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Woe to every slanderer and mocker﴾ [al-Humazah: 1]. From this is also His saying: ﴿And among them are those who criticize you concerning the charities﴾ [al-Tawbah: 58]. The majority recited "talmizu" with a kasra on the mim, while al-A'raj and al-Hasan recited it with a damma. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "It is Arabic; our recitation is with a damma, and sometimes with a kasra."

His saying, "anfusakum" (your souls), means "some of you toward others," as in His saying: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29]. It is as if the believers are one soul, since they are brothers. So, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "They are like the body: when one of its limbs complains, the rest of it responds with sleeplessness and fever." And he also said: "They are like a building, one part of which strengthens another."

"Tanabuz" is calling by nicknames. "Nabz" and "laqab" are the same, since a laqab is the name by which a person is known, which he dislikes to hear. It is related that the Banu Salamah had many nicknames among them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called a man from among them and said, "O so-and-so." It was said to him, "He becomes angry at this name." Then he called another in the same way, and the verse was revealed concerning this. It is not included in this what the narrators say, such as "Sulayman al-A'mash" (the one with weak eyes) and "Wasil al-Ahdab" (the hunchback). Similar things, which necessity calls for, and in which there is no intention of contempt or harm, are permitted. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said to 'Alqamah, "Do you say that, O one-eyed man?" Al-Naqqash related through 'Ata' that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Restrain your children," meaning, 'Ata' said, out of fear of nicknames. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of "and do not insult one another with nicknames" is that no one should say to another, "O Jew," after his Islam, or "O sinner," after his repentance, and the like. Al-Naqqash related that Ka'b ibn Malik and Ibn Abi Hadrad quarrelled, and Ka'b said to him, "O Bedouin," intending to distance him from the emigration (hijrah). The other said to him, "O Jew," because of the Ansar's association with the Jews in Yathrib. Then the verse was revealed.

His saying, ﴿Wretched is the name of defiance after belief﴾, may have two meanings. One: wretched is the name you acquire through your disobedience and your calling of one another by nicknames, so that you become sinners through disobedience after your belief. The second: wretched is what a man says to his brother, "O sinner," after his belief. Al-Rummani said: this verse indicates that defiance and belief cannot coexist. This is a Mu'tazili tendency. Then Allah the Exalted intensified the prohibition upon them by ruling that whoever does not repent and desist from these things which He has forbidden is a wrongdoer.

Then the Blessed and Exalted commanded the believers to avoid much assumption, and not to act or speak in accordance with it, because of what that and spying entail of severing ties and mutual aversion. He ruled that some of it is sin, since some of it is not sin and need not be avoided, and that is assuming good of people. Good assumption about Allah the Exalted is good. Also, what is assumed from the testimony of witnesses, and what is assumed of people of evil, if that leads to the loss of his uprightness, and similar matters, are part of the ruling on assumption about them. Assuming good of a believer is praiseworthy. The assumption that is forbidden is that you assume evil of a man whose outward appearance is righteousness. Rather, the duty is to remove the assumption and its ruling, and to interpret things in the best way. Some people said: "sin" (ithm) means falsehood, and from this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Beware of assumption, for assumption is the most false of speech." Some people said: the meaning of His saying, ﴿Indeed some assumption is sin﴾, is that if the one assuming speaks, he sins, but as long as he does not speak he is at ease, because he cannot prevent the thoughts that the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) permits: "Caution is the evil of assumption."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

People of knowledge have never ceased to guard against evil assumption and to block its avenues. Salman al-Farisi said: "Indeed I count the ring of my pot out of fear of assumption." Abu al-'Aliyah would seal the remainder of his food out of fear of evil assumption about his servant. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Trustworthiness is better than a seal ring, and a seal ring is better than evil assumption."

His saying, "wa la tajassasu" (and do not spy), means: do not search out the hidden affairs of people. Repel with what is best, and be content with the good outward appearances. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Ibn Sirin, and the Hudhayl recited "wa la tahassasu" with an unpointed ha'. Some people said: tajassus with the jim is in evil, and tahassus with the ha' is in good. Thus the Qur'an came, but they may overlap in usage. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: tajassus is what is done from behind a screen, and tahassus is entering and seeking information. It is authentically related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Do not seek out (tahassasu) and do not spy (tajassasu), do not envy, do not turn away from one another, and be, O servants of Allah, brothers." Al-Tha'labi mentioned the hadith about 'Umar ibn al-Khattab's night patrol with Ibn 'Awf, may Allah be pleased with them both, and their finding of drinking in the house of Rabi'ah ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf. He also mentioned his hadith on this with Abu Mihjan al-Thaqafi. Zayd ibn Wahb said: It was said to Ibn Mas'ud, "Would you like [to know about] al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah, whose beard is dripping with wine?" He said: "We have been forbidden from spying. If something becomes apparent to us, we will act upon it."

His saying, "wa la yaghtab" (and let not one of you backbite another), means: let none of you mention about his brother something in him that he dislikes to hear. It is related that 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said about a woman, "I have never seen anyone more beautiful than her, except that she is short." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to her, "You have backbitten her; you looked at the worst thing in her and mentioned it." The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "If you mention what is in your brother, you have backbitten him, and if you mention what is not in him, you have slandered him." In another hadith: "Backbiting is that you mention a believer with what he dislikes." It was said: "Even if it is true?" He said: "If you say what is false, that is slander (buhtan)." Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah and Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i said: If a man with amputated limbs passes you and you say, "That amputee," that is backbiting. These verses and those that follow were revealed concerning the character of the people of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance). That is because they followed the desires of their souls, and no command or prohibition from Allah the Exalted restrained them. Some have said it derives from "qiyam" (standing), or is the plural of "qa'im" (standing) as "da'if" (weak). From this is the verse of the poet, Zuhayr:

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 49, verses 13–14:**

The words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic:

﴿O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female and made you nations (shu'ub) and tribes (qaba'il) that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you. Indeed, Allah is Knowing, Acquainted.﴾ ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; but say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts. And if you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not deprive you of anything of your deeds. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."﴾

His words, ﴿from male and female﴾, may mean Adam and Eve, peace be upon them, so it is as if He, the Exalted, said: "We created you all from Adam and Eve." It may also mean that "male and female" is a generic term (ism al-jins), as if He, the Exalted, said: "We created each one of you from a drop of male and female water." The purpose of this verse is the equality of people. Then the Exalted says, ﴿and made you nations and tribes that you may know one another﴾, meaning, so that you do not boast, and so that some of you do not wish to be more honourable than others, for the path to honour is other than this, ﴿indeed the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾. Abu Bakra narrated: "It was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, who is the best of people?' He said: 'The one whose life is long and whose deeds are good.'" In another hadith: "Who is the best of people?' He said: 'The one who is most enjoining of what is right, most forbidding of what is wrong, most keeping of the ties of kinship, and most righteous.'"

Al-Zahrawi related that the occasion of revelation of this verse was the anger of al-Harith ibn Hisham and 'Attab ibn Usayd when Bilal called the adhan upon the Ka'ba on the day of the Conquest of Makkah. Al-Tha'labi related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that its occasion was "the saying of Thabit ibn Qays to a man who had not been given room near the Prophet ﷺ: 'O son of so-and-so,' so the Prophet ﷺ rebuked him and said to him: 'You do not prefer anyone except in religion and piety.' Then this verse was revealed," and the command to make room for others was also revealed concerning that.

"Shu'ub" is the plural of sha'b (people/nation, the broadest grouping), which is the largest of the gatherings of people linked by one lineage. It is followed by the qabila (tribe), then the 'imara (clan), then the batn (sub-clan), then the fakhdh (lineage group), then the usra (family) and the fasila (immediate household), and these two are a man's closest kin. Thus Mudar, Rabi'a and Himyar are shu'ub; Qays, Tamim, Madhhij and Murad are qaba'il, likened to the "tribes of the head" because they are separate pieces that face one another; Quraysh and Muharib are 'imarat; Banu Qusayy and Banu Makhzum are butun; Banu Hashim, Banu Umayya and the like are afkhadh; and Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib is an usra and fasila. Ibn Jubayr said: "The shu'ub are the afkhadh."

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "the shu'ub are the butun," but this is not what the linguists have agreed upon. Al-Tha'labi said: "It was said: the shu'ub are among non-Arabs, the qaba'il among Arabs, and the asbat among the Children of Israel. As for the Sha'b in Hamadan, from which al-Sha'bi is named, it is a batn called al-Sha'b. It was also said that the nations that are not Arab are called 'Shu'ubiyya,' a designation derived from shu'ub, because the detail of their lineages was obscure, so none of them was known except by saying: Persian, Turk, Roman. It is as if they were known by their shu'ub, which is the most general term used to express their groups. They are called al-Shu'ubiyya with a fatha on the shin, and this is a change in the nisba. Other things have been said about them besides what I have mentioned, but this is preferable in my view."

Al-A'mash recited "li-tata'arafu" (with two taa'). 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, recited "li-ta'rifu anna" on the pattern of "taf'alu," with a kasra on the 'ayn and a fatha on the alif of "anna," with "ta'rifu" governing it. According to this reading, the lam in His words "li-ta'rifu" may be the lam of purpose (lam kay), and the meaning is somewhat altered by this. It may also be the lam of command (lam al-amr), which is better in meaning. And the object may be omitted, its estimate being "the truth." If it is the lam of purpose, it is as if He, the Exalted, said: "O mankind, you are equal insofar as you are created. You were made into tribes only so that you may know one another and so that you may know the realities. As for nobility and honour, it is by the piety of Allah, the Exalted, and the soundness of hearts." Ibn Mas'ud recited: "li-ta'arafu baynakum, wa khayrukum 'inda Allahi atqakum." It is related that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever would like to be the most honourable of people, let him fear Allah, his Lord." Then the Exalted alerted to caution with His words, ﴿indeed Allah is Knowing, Acquainted﴾, meaning, of the one who is pious and deserves the rank of honour.

His words, the Exalted, ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed"﴾: Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning the Banu Asad ibn Khuzayma, a tribe that lived near Madinah. They had openly professed Islam, but their souls, despite that, were corrupt (dakhila), loving only spoils and worldly goods. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "They once went so far as to try to attribute themselves to the Muhajirun, so this verse was revealed, naming them 'Bedouins,' informing them of their true standing, and bringing out into the open the forms of belief hidden in their breasts. They are specific Bedouins, as we have mentioned." Abu Hatim related from Ibn al-Zubayr: "The Prophet ﷺ heard a man recite: 'Qalati al-a'rabu' without a hamza, and he corrected him with a hamzat qat' (a clear hamza)." Allah, the Exalted, has informed that He should say to these claimants to faith: ﴿You have not believed﴾, meaning, you have not affirmed with your hearts, ﴿but say, "We have submitted"﴾.

Islam (al-islam) is used in two senses. One comprises both faith and deeds, and it is the sense in His words, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19], and in His, ﴿Islam is built upon five﴾, and in the Prophet's ﷺ teaching of Jibril, peace be upon him, when he "said: 'What is Islam?' He said: 'That you worship Allah alone and associate nothing with Him, establish the prayer, pay the zakat, fast Ramadan, and make pilgrimage to the House if you are able to find a way to it.'" And it is the sense in "the Prophet's ﷺ saying to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him: 'Or a Muslim. Indeed, I give to a man while another is dearer to me than him,'" the hadith. This Islam is not the one in His words, the Exalted, ﴿but say, "We have submitted"﴾. The second meaning of the word Islam is submission (al-istislam) and outward declaration by which one is protected and by which blood is spared, and this is the Islam in His words, the Exalted, ﴿but say, "We have submitted"﴾. Faith, which is affirmation (al-tasdiq), is more specific than the first.

Then the Exalted explicitly told them that faith had not entered their hearts, and then He opened for them the door of repentance by His words, the Glorified, ﴿And if you obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ (the verse), and obedience to Allah, the Exalted, and His Messenger ﷺ includes within it both faith and deeds.

The majority of reciters read "la yalitkum" (from "lata yalitu," meaning to diminish), as in "latahu haqqahu" when he diminished it from him. Abu 'Amr, al-A'raj, al-Hasan and 'Amr read "la ya'altikum" from "alata ya'iltu," which has the same meaning as "lata." Likewise it is said "alita" with a kasra on the lam, "ya'iltu," and it is also said with the same meaning as "lata": "alata yulitu," but no one recited with this dialect. The rest of the verse is clear in its meaning of reassurance (al-tarjiya).

Al-Tha'labi said: "It was said: the shu'ub are among non-Arabs, the qaba'il among Arabs, and the asbat among the Children of Israel. As for the Sha'b in Hamadan, from which al-Sha'bi is named, it is a batn called al-Sha'b. It was also said that the nations that are not Arab are called 'Shu'ubiyya,' a designation derived from shu'ub, because the detail of their lineages was obscure, so none of them was known except by saying: Persian, Turk, Roman. It is as if they were known by their shu'ub, which is the most general term used to express their groups. They are called al-Shu'ubiyya with a fatha on the shin, and this is a change in the nisba. Other things have been said about them besides what I have mentioned, but this is preferable in my view."

Al-A'mash recited "li-tata'arafu" (with two taa'). 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, recited "li-ta'rifu anna" on the pattern of "taf'alu," with a kasra on the 'ayn and a fatha on the alif of "anna," with "ta'rifu" governing it. According to this reading, the lam in His words "li-ta'rifu" may be the lam of purpose (lam kay), and the meaning is somewhat altered by this. It may also be the lam of command (lam al-amr), which is better in meaning. And the object may be omitted, its estimate being "the truth." If it is the lam of purpose, it is as if He, the Exalted, said: "O mankind, you are equal insofar as you are created. You were made into tribes only so that you may know one another and so that you may know the realities. As for nobility and honour, it is by the piety of Allah, the Exalted, and the soundness of hearts." Ibn Mas'ud recited: "li-ta'arafu baynakum, wa khayrukum 'inda Allahi atqakum." It is related that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever would like to be the most honourable of people, let him fear Allah, his Lord." Then the Exalted alerted to caution with His words, ﴿indeed Allah is Knowing, Acquainted﴾, meaning, of the one who is pious and deserves the rank of honour.

His words, the Exalted, ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed"﴾: Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning the Banu Asad ibn Khuzayma, a tribe that lived near Madinah. They had openly professed Islam, but their souls, despite that, were corrupt (dakhila), loving only spoils and worldly goods. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "They once went so far as to try to attribute themselves to the Muhajirun, so this verse was revealed, naming them 'Bedouins,' informing them of their true standing, and bringing out into the open the forms of belief hidden in their breasts. They are specific Bedouins, as we have mentioned." Abu Hatim related from Ibn al-Zubayr: "The Prophet ﷺ heard a man recite: 'Qalati al-a'rabu' without a hamza, and he corrected him with a hamzat qat' (a clear hamza)." Allah, the Exalted, has informed that He should say to these claimants to faith: ﴿You have not believed﴾, meaning, you have not affirmed with your hearts, ﴿but say, "We have submitted"﴾.

Islam (al-islam) is used in two senses. One comprises both faith and deeds, and it is the sense in His words, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19], and in His, ﴿Islam is built upon five﴾, and in the Prophet's ﷺ teaching of Jibril, peace be upon him, when he "said: 'What is Islam?' He said: 'That you worship Allah alone and associate nothing with Him, establish the prayer, pay the zakat, fast Ramadan, and make pilgrimage to the House if you are able to find a way to it.'" And it is the sense in "the Prophet's ﷺ saying to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him: 'Or a Muslim. Indeed, I give to a man while another is dearer to me than him,'" the hadith. This Islam is not the one in His words, the Exalted, ﴿but say, "We have submitted"﴾. The second meaning of the word Islam is submission (al-istislam) and outward declaration by which one is protected and by which blood is spared, and this is the Islam in His words, the Exalted, ﴿but say, "We have submitted"﴾. Faith, which is affirmation (al-tasdiq), is more specific than the first.

Then the Exalted explicitly told them that faith had not entered their hearts, and then He opened for them the door of repentance by His words, the Glorified, ﴿And if you obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ (the verse), and obedience to Allah, the Exalted, and His Messenger ﷺ includes within it both faith and deeds.

The majority of reciters read "la yalitkum" (from "lata yalitu," meaning to diminish), as in "latahu haqqahu" when he diminished it from him. Abu 'Amr, al-A'raj, al-Hasan and 'Amr read "la ya'altikum" from "alata ya'iltu," which has the same meaning as "lata." Likewise it is said "alita" with a kasra on the lam, "ya'iltu," and it is also said with the same meaning as "lata": "alata yulitu," but no one recited with this dialect. The rest of the verse is clear in its meaning of reassurance (al-tarjiya).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 49, verse 15–18:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿The believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger and then have not doubted but strove with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah. Those are the truthful.﴾ ﴿Say: "Will you inform Allah of your religion, while Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and Allah is Knowing of all things?"﴾ ﴿They consider it a favor to you that they have accepted Islam. Say: "Do not consider your Islam a favor to me. Rather, Allah has conferred favor upon you that He guided you to faith, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

"Innama" (only) in this verse is restrictive, conveying that meaning. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then they have not doubted﴾ means: they did not doubt their faith, and no uncertainty entered them. ﴿And those are the truthful﴾, since their actions came to confirm their words. Then Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet ﷺ to rebuke them with His saying: ﴿Will you inform Allah of your religion?﴾, meaning by your saying "We have believed," while He knows from you the opposite of that, for He is the All-Knowing of all things.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They consider it a favor to you that they have accepted Islam﴾ was revealed concerning the Banu Asad as well. That is because they said to the Prophet ﷺ at some times: "We have believed in you and followed you, and we did not fight against you as Muharib, Hasfa, Hawazin, Ghatafan and others did." So this verse was revealed. This is related by al-Tabari and others. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, recited: "They consider it a favor to you, their Islam (yumannuna 'alayka islamahu)."

His saying, exalted is He, "an" may be a maf'ul li-ajlihi (object of purpose). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Rather, Allah has conferred favor upon you that He guided you to faith﴾ means: according to your claim, since you say "We have believed." It is then necessarily binding upon you that Allah, exalted is He, has bestowed favor upon you. What indicates this meaning is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿if you are truthful﴾, whereby He conditioned both rulings upon them: they are the ones upon whom favor is bestowed if they are truthful, and it is fitting for them to say "We have accepted Islam" only if they are truthful, not if they are liars.

Ibn Mas'ud recited: "idh hadakum (when He guided you)."

His saying, exalted is He, "yamunnu 'alaykum" may mean: "yun'im" (bestows blessing), as you say: "Allah has favored you (manna Allahu 'alayka)." It may also mean: "yadhkuru ihsanahu" (He mentions His benevolence), so that it stands in parallel to "yamunnuna 'alayka." The people of old said: "When blessing is ungrateful, the reminder of favor becomes good." What nullifies charity as a disliked act is only the reminder of favor that occurs short of ingratitude for blessing.

Abu Ja'far, Nafi', Shayba, Qatada and Ibn Wathhab recited "ta'malun" with the ta' (second person address). Ibn Kathir and 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, recited "ya'malun" with the ya' from below, referring to the third person.

The commentary of Surat al-Hujurat is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
